questions.stem: The first recorded gladiatorial fight at Rome, in 264 BCE, was held:
options: to celebrate the opening of the Flavian Amphitheatre
by the Senate to mark the end of the Punic Wars
as part of the yearly festival of the god Jupiter
at the funeral of a nobleman, given by his sons
questions.explanation: Ancient writers record that the sons of Decimus Junius Brutus Pera staged fights between pairs of gladiators at his funeral in 264 BCE. The Flavian Amphitheatre opened more than three centuries later.

questions.stem: The Romans called gladiatorial shows munera. The word, meaning 'duties' or 'gifts', reflects the fact that the shows:
options: were held only as rewards for soldiers returning from campaigns
were presents given by foreign kings to the Roman Senate
began as obligations owed to the dead and became gifts to the people
were always paid for by the state treasury as part of the religious law
questions.explanation: Munera were first a duty to honour a dead relative, and later shows were presented as gifts by magistrates and emperors. Ludi, such as chariot races, were public festivals linked to the gods.

questions.stem: Ancient and modern writers disagree about where gladiatorial combat came from. Which statement best reflects the evidence?
options: Some writers credit the Etruscans; Campanian tomb paintings suggest southern Italy
All sources agree it was brought to Rome from Egypt by Julius Caesar
Gladiatorial combat began in Greece and was copied directly from the Olympic Games
It was invented by Augustus as part of his new imperial ceremonies
questions.explanation: Some ancient writers credited the Etruscans, while funeral paintings of armed duels from Campania and Lucania point to southern Italy. The question remains debated, but the shows were well established long before Caesar or Augustus.

questions.stem: An amphitheatre differs from a circus because an amphitheatre is:
options: long and narrow, with a central barrier for chariot racing
semicircular, facing a stage for plays and concerts
square, with covered walkways used for public meetings
oval, with seats all round an arena for fights and hunts
questions.explanation: The oval amphitheatre suited gladiator fights and beast hunts. The long circus with its central barrier was for chariot races, and the semicircular theatre was for drama.

questions.stem: Before the first permanent stone amphitheatre was built in Rome in 29 BCE, gladiatorial shows in the city were usually held:
options: on the Campus Martius, inside the army's barracks
in the Forum, with temporary wooden stands
inside temples, before the statue of Jupiter
in the Senate house, before the senators only
questions.explanation: Shows in Rome were long held in the Forum with temporary wooden seating. The stone amphitheatre built by Statilius Taurus in 29 BCE was the first permanent one in the city.

questions.stem: Amphitheatres survive at Nimes in Gaul, El Djem in North Africa and Caerleon in Britain. What does their distribution show?
options: The games spread across the provinces as part of Roman urban life
Gladiators were trained only in the provinces, never in Italy
The games were banned in Rome itself and so moved out to the frontiers
Every amphitheatre was built by the emperor Nero in one year
questions.explanation: Amphitheatres in towns and army bases from Britain to North Africa show the games spreading with Roman culture, especially in the West. Rome itself remained the greatest centre of the games.

questions.stem: In 27 CE a wooden amphitheatre at Fidenae, near Rome, collapsed during a show, killing or injuring many spectators. According to Tacitus, the Senate's response was to:
options: order that only the emperor could ever build an amphitheatre in future
move all gladiatorial shows to the Circus Maximus for safety
set rules on the wealth of show-givers and on the soundness of buildings
ban all gladiatorial games throughout Italy for the rest of Tiberius's reign
questions.explanation: Tacitus reports that the Senate required those staging shows to have a minimum fortune and that amphitheatres be built on sound ground. The disaster encouraged the move towards stone buildings.

questions.stem: The Flavian Amphitheatre (the Colosseum) was begun by Vespasian and dedicated in 80 CE by:
options: Trajan, after his conquest of Dacia
his son Titus, with 100 days of games
Nero, as part of his Golden House
Augustus, to celebrate the victory at Actium
questions.explanation: Vespasian began the amphitheatre in the 70s CE on the site of the lake of Nero's Golden House, and Titus opened it in 80 CE with 100 days of games. Domitian completed further work, including the underground hypogeum.

questions.stem: Vespasian built the Flavian Amphitheatre on land that had been part of Nero's Golden House. The main political message was that:
options: Nero's memory should be honoured with the largest building in Rome
the Senate would now control all public buildings in the city
land taken for one emperor's pleasure was returned to the people
the new dynasty planned to rebuild Nero's palace on a larger scale
questions.explanation: Placing a public entertainment building on Nero's private estate presented the Flavians as generous to the people, in contrast with Nero. The amphitheatre was paid for largely with spoils of the Jewish War.

questions.stem: Beneath the arena floor of the Flavian Amphitheatre lay the hypogeum. It was used to:
options: seat the emperor and his family safely below the crowd
hold animals, fighters and scenery, raised into the arena by lifts
store the water used for flooding the arena for every naval battle
bury the gladiators who died in the shows each day
questions.explanation: The hypogeum was a network of passages and cages with lifts and trapdoors that brought animals and scenery into the arena for dramatic effect. Most scholars think its construction ended any flooding of the arena for naval shows.

questions.stem: Seating in the Flavian Amphitheatre was arranged so that:
options: senators sat nearest the arena and women and the poor sat at the top
anyone could sit anywhere, since all citizens were treated as equals
slaves had the best seats, as they were the gladiators' families
the emperor sat in the highest row, furthest from the arena
questions.explanation: Seating followed rank, a rule Augustus had set out, with senators at the front, equites behind, then citizens, and women and the poorest at the top. The emperor had a box at the arena's edge.

questions.stem: The Circus Maximus in Rome was mainly used for:
options: theatre performances of Greek and Roman plays
naval battles staged in its flooded arena
chariot races around a central barrier called the spina
gladiator fights between the main types of armed gladiator
questions.explanation: The Circus Maximus was a long track in the valley between the Palatine and Aventine Hills, the largest venue for public entertainment in Rome. Chariots raced around the spina, turning at posts called metae.

questions.stem: The Gladiator Mosaic found at Torrenova near Rome, now in the Galleria Borghese, labels fighters by name and marks some with the Greek letter theta. Why is it valuable evidence?
options: It proves that every gladiator fight ended in the loser's death
It was painted by an eyewitness at the Colosseum's opening in 80 CE
It shows named fighters, their equipment and which of them died
It records the exact number of spectators at each show in Rome
questions.explanation: The mosaic, from the fourth century CE, names gladiators and beast fighters and marks the dead with theta, for thanatos (death). It shows equipment and outcomes, but not every fighter in it died, which itself is evidence.

questions.stem: The satirist Juvenal complained that the Roman people, who once gave out military commands and offices, now longed for only two things. These were:
options: land and citizenship
wine and gladiators
peace and lower taxes
bread and circuses
questions.explanation: In his tenth Satire Juvenal mocks the people for wanting only 'bread and circuses' (panem et circenses), meaning free food and entertainment. Historians use the phrase to discuss how the games kept the urban population content.

questions.stem: Juvenal's phrase 'bread and circuses' is often quoted as proof that emperors used the games to control the people. What is the main limitation of using it this way?
options: It is a Christian text written to condemn the Roman emperors
It is an official law of Augustus, so it shows only his own aims
It is satire meant to mock, so it exaggerates and reflects an elite view
Juvenal lived before any games were held, so he could never have seen them
questions.explanation: Juvenal was a satirist writing for an educated audience, so his comment is an exaggerated, upper-class complaint rather than a neutral analysis. It is still useful evidence of attitudes.

questions.stem: Martial's Book of Spectacles is a collection of short poems that:
options: condemned the games as immoral and called on Romans to abandon them
recorded the detailed rules of chariot racing for the four circus factions
listed the laws governing the training of gladiators
celebrated the shows given at the opening of the Flavian Amphitheatre
questions.explanation: Martial wrote praise poems on the spectacles of the Flavian emperor, probably Titus's opening games in 80 CE, including beast hunts and executions. As flattery of the emperor, they must be read with care.

questions.stem: Martial describes two gladiators, Priscus and Verus, who fought to a standstill at the Colosseum's opening games. The emperor's response was to:
options: order both men to be put to death for failing to finish the fight properly
make both men fight wild animals until one of them had died
send both men to the mines for the rest of their lives
grant both men the wooden sword of freedom and the palm of victory
questions.explanation: According to Martial, the emperor gave both the rudis (the wooden sword that marked release) and palms. The story shows that a brave fight, not a death, could please the crowd and the emperor.

questions.stem: Seneca, in a letter to Lucilius, says he went to the midday show expecting some light relief and found instead pure killing. What does this source best show?
options: Some educated Romans criticised the games, mainly for their effect on the crowd
All Romans opposed the games, so the emperors held them in secret
The midday shows involved only highly trained gladiators who rarely died
Seneca wanted the games made more violent to entertain the people
questions.explanation: Seneca describes the midday executions of condemned men and worries that such spectacles corrupt the spectators. His view was not typical of most Romans, who enjoyed the games.

questions.stem: Epigraphic sources such as tombstones and painted notices are valuable for the study of the games because they:
options: were all written by the emperors and give only the official view of the games
describe every show held in the Flavian Amphitheatre in full
were composed by Christian bishops who attended the games
record gladiators' names, fights and families, beyond elite literature
questions.explanation: Gladiators' epitaphs, often set up by wives or comrades, record their type, number of fights and age at death, while painted notices advertised shows. They give voices that literary sources ignore.

questions.stem: In his Res Gestae, Augustus records that he gave gladiatorial shows in which about 10,000 men fought. How should a historian interpret this claim?
options: As a boast showing that generous games were part of his public image
As proof that 10,000 gladiators died in a single show in Rome
As a complaint that the games were too costly for the treasury
As evidence that Augustus banned the games after his victory at Actium
questions.explanation: Augustus listed his shows among his achievements, which shows how the games served his image as benefactor of the Roman people. The figure is a total across several shows, and most fighters did not die.

questions.stem: A naumachia was:
options: a beast hunt held in an artificial forest
a procession of all the gladiators before the games began
a staged naval battle fought on a lake or flooded basin
a chariot race run with four horses abreast
questions.explanation: Julius Caesar and Augustus dug basins for naval battles, Claudius staged one on the Fucine Lake, and ancient writers say Titus flooded an arena for one at the opening games. The fighters were usually condemned men or prisoners.

questions.stem: Chariot racing teams in Rome were organised into factions known by their colours. The four colours were:
options: red, white, green and blue
gold, silver, purple and black
red, yellow, purple and white
black, green, orange and blue
questions.explanation: The Reds, Whites, Greens and Blues had passionate supporters. By late antiquity the Blues and Greens dominated, and their rivalry later fuelled riots in Constantinople.

questions.stem: Why were successful charioteers among the most famous people in Rome, even though many began as slaves?
options: The law ranked charioteers above priests and magistrates
Only members of the emperor's own family were allowed to race chariots
Victories brought them huge prize money, fame and devoted fans
They were automatically made senators after ten wins
questions.explanation: Inscriptions record charioteers such as Diocles winning vast sums, and fans followed them and their factions closely. Their low legal status did not prevent great popularity.

questions.stem: Venationes were shows in which:
options: gladiators on horseback raced one another around the arena
trained actors performed short comedies between the morning fights
wild animals were hunted and killed, or made to fight each other
condemned prisoners were made to fight each other with swords
questions.explanation: Beast hunts, often in the morning, displayed exotic animals such as lions, leopards and elephants, brought from across the empire. Hunters called venatores fought them.

questions.stem: Huge numbers of wild animals were brought to Rome from Africa and Asia for the games. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The hunts displayed Roman power and harmed some animal populations
The animals were mostly bred in Italy, so the games had no effect elsewhere
Beast hunts were rare, held only once in each emperor's reign
Animals were never killed, only displayed in parades for the crowd
questions.explanation: Bringing exotic beasts from distant provinces showed the extent of Roman rule, and heavy hunting is thought to have reduced animals such as lions in North Africa. Hunts were frequent, and the animals were usually killed.

questions.stem: A retiarius fought with:
options: two swords, one held in each hand
a net, a trident and a dagger, with no helmet
a large shield, a short sword and a crested helmet
a curved sword and a small square shield
questions.explanation: The retiarius was lightly armed, with a net to entangle his opponent and a trident to strike from a distance. The other kits describe the murmillo, the thraex and the dimachaerus.

questions.stem: The retiarius was usually matched against the secutor, who wore a smooth, rounded helmet with small eye holes. Why was this helmet suited to that pairing?
options: It gave the net and trident little to catch on or get through
It let the secutor see far behind him to avoid ambushes
It was very light, so the secutor could throw it as a weapon
It showed the crowd which gladiator was the emperor's favourite
questions.explanation: The smooth helmet had no crest or rim for a net to snag, and the small eye holes resisted the trident's points, though they limited the secutor's vision. Pairings balanced different strengths for a good contest.

questions.stem: The murmillo, with a large rectangular shield and a short sword, was often matched against the thraex. How did the thraex's equipment differ?
options: He carried a net and trident and wore no armour
He fought from a chariot with a long spear
He wore no helmet and fought only with his bare fists
He carried a small shield and a short curved sword
questions.explanation: The thraex (Thracian) had a small shield and a curved sica, making him more mobile but less protected than the heavily shielded murmillo. Pairings contrasted heavy and light styles.

questions.stem: A gladiator school (ludus) was run by a lanista. The lanista's role was to:
options: judge the fight and decide the loser's fate
lead the procession as priest of the games
collect the entry fees from all the spectators
own, train and hire out a troupe of gladiators
questions.explanation: The lanista bought, trained and hired out gladiators to those staging shows. The giver of the games (the editor) decided whether a defeated fighter was spared.

questions.stem: Skeletons from a gladiator cemetery at Ephesus show healed wounds and a diet rich in grains and beans. What can a historian best conclude?
options: Gladiators were vegetarian for religious reasons set by the emperors
Gladiators were valuable, so owners fed them and paid for medical care
Gladiators were starved to make them fierce before each fight
Every gladiator was killed in his very first fight, without any treatment
questions.explanation: Healed injuries point to medical treatment, and a carbohydrate-rich diet may have built protective body fat, which fits ancient references to gladiators as 'barley men'. Trained fighters were costly investments, so many survived several bouts.

questions.stem: Gladiators held a contradictory status in Roman society. Which statement best describes it?
options: They were despised by everyone and never shown in Roman art
They were priests whose fights were seen only as religious rituals
They were legally disgraced (infamis) yet admired as heroes by many
They were all citizens of high rank, honoured with seats in the Senate
questions.explanation: Gladiators bore infamia, a legal disgrace shared with actors and prostitutes, yet graffiti, lamps and mosaics show them as celebrities admired for courage. Some free men even signed on voluntarily.

questions.stem: Some free Roman men chose to become gladiators, taking an oath to submit to their owner. Which reason is best supported by the sources?
options: Gladiators were exempt from all taxes and could not be killed
Becoming a gladiator was a common path for poor men into the Senate
Debt or poverty, with the chance of a signing fee, prize money and fame
The law required every citizen to serve one year as a gladiator
questions.explanation: Volunteers (auctorati) received a payment and could win money and glory, which drew men in debt or seeking fame. They gave up their legal standing, so no law compelled it.

questions.stem: Condemned criminals in the arena (noxii) were often executed during the midday shows by:
options: being freed if they could finish a chariot race
being exiled to an island after appearing in a procession
being exposed to wild animals or forced to fight unarmed
being trained for years before fighting as skilled gladiators
questions.explanation: Executions, including damnatio ad bestias (condemnation to the beasts), were part of the midday programme. Unlike trained gladiators, the condemned had no real chance of survival.

questions.stem: Which group of victims of the games is recorded in Christian sources such as the account of Perpetua and Felicity at Carthage?
options: Priests of Jupiter sacrificed at the end of each show
Christians condemned to the beasts for refusing to sacrifice
Senators executed for supporting the wrong chariot faction
Gladiators punished for losing a fight to a woman fighter
questions.explanation: The Passion of Perpetua and Felicity describes the women's deaths in the arena at Carthage in 203 CE. Such martyr accounts are valuable but were written to inspire believers.

questions.stem: Why did Republican politicians such as Julius Caesar spend vast sums on games while holding office as aedile?
options: To win popularity and votes for election to higher office
Because the law required every aedile to fight in the arena
To raise money for the treasury from ticket sales
To train an army of gladiators for foreign wars
questions.explanation: Lavish games built a politician's support among voters. Suetonius reports that the Senate limited the number of gladiators Caesar could show as aedile, fearing a private armed force.

questions.stem: Under the emperors, the crowd in the amphitheatre and circus could shout demands to the emperor in person. Historians use this to argue that the games:
options: were used mainly to recruit soldiers for the legions
were a place where ruler met people and his popularity was tested
had no political role at all, since the emperor never attended them in person
allowed the crowd to vote on new laws in place of the Senate
questions.explanation: The games were a rare setting where the emperor faced the people, who could cheer, complain or petition him. Emperors such as Titus won favour by attending and granting requests, while Commodus damaged his reputation by fighting in the arena.

questions.stem: Which explanation of the decline of gladiatorial games is most defensible?
options: Christian criticism, the cost of shows and changing tastes all mattered
Gladiators went on strike and refused to fight at all after the third century
The Flavian Amphitheatre was destroyed in 80 CE, ending all games
Augustus banned the games, and no shows were held after his death
questions.explanation: Constantine expressed disapproval in 325 CE, Christian writers attacked the shows, and the cost of games rose as the economy weakened. Gladiatorial combat faded in the early fifth century, while beast hunts and chariot racing lasted longer.

questions.stem: After gladiatorial combat ended, which form of entertainment continued for the longest, especially in Constantinople?
options: Executions of the condemned by beasts
Chariot racing in the hippodrome
Naval battles on flooded lakes
Fights between pairs of gladiators
questions.explanation: Chariot racing remained hugely popular in the eastern empire, and the Blue and Green factions played a part in the Nika riots of 532 CE. Gladiatorial fights had ended over a century earlier.

questions.stem: Jean-Leon Gerome's painting Pollice Verso (1872) shows spectators turning their thumbs down to call for a gladiator's death. Why should historians treat this image with caution?
options: It was painted from a photograph taken in the Colosseum in ancient times
Roman sources state clearly that a thumbs-down gesture meant the loser was spared
The painting shows a chariot race, not a gladiatorial fight
The exact gesture is uncertain, and the painting reflects a 19th-century view
questions.explanation: Latin sources mention a turned thumb but do not make clear which way meant death, so the famous thumbs-down image comes largely from this painting. It has strongly shaped modern films such as Gladiator.

questions.stem: Films such as Gladiator (2000) show almost every fight ending in death. Which evidence best challenges this representation?
options: Epitaphs record many fights, and sources describe defeated men being spared
Roman law made it a serious crime for any gladiator to be killed in the arena
The games were bloodless displays of skill, as Seneca describes them
No gladiator ever fought more than once in his whole career
questions.explanation: Tombstones list fighters with many bouts, and a defeated gladiator could be granted missio (release), since trained men were costly. Seneca describes the midday killings as brutal, not bloodless.
